system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 23 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-05-01 07:15:00 to 2154-05-23 17:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for planned initiation of hemodialysis due to end-stage renal disease from polycystic kidney disease. She reported symptoms of fluid overload including leg swelling, dyspnea on exertion, and abdominal discomfort from enlarged kidneys. She underwent three hemodialysis sessions without complications and showed clinical improvement in volume status and breathing. Medications were adjusted, including discontinuation of atenolol, valsartan, furosemide, darbepoetin, iron, and hectorol, with continuation of amiodarone, coumadin, lisinopril, and amlodipine. A chest X-ray showed no pulmonary congestion. The patient tolerated the transition well, was stable at discharge, and returned home with follow-up arranged. DNR/DNI status was discussed and documented.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery

Brief Hospital Course:
___ y/o female with polycystic kidney disease who underwent 
bilateral native nephrectomies with Dr ___.
Per the operative report there were multiple hernias in this 
area. numerous pieces of mesh were encountered as the abdomen 
was entered and there were a significant
amount of adhesions. Once the kidneys were isolated, the 
adrenals were spared and the kidneys were removed. Of note they 
were approximately 8 kg in weight with multiple large cysts. All 
of the mesh was removed and the hernias were repaired primarily.
In the post op period on POD 2 she was noted to be very 
lethargic and had developed a fever to 101.6. Due to her mental 
status a stroke consult was called
MRI and MRA of the head were done showing that the bilateral 
internal carotid arteries and their major branches appear normal 
without evidence of stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm formation. 
The report was read as no acute hemorrhage or infarction seen. 
No perfusion abnormalities detected. 
There was stenosis of the right vertebral artery at the origin 
of the ___.
Blood cultures were sent that were negative.
On POD 6 she developed diarrhea, cdiff culture was sent which 
came back positive. She was initially started on Flagyl 
monotherapy, but Dr ___ recommended dual therapy with IV 
Flagyl and PO Vanco which was continued throughout the 
hospitalization. ID was consulted and they recommended 
continuing the PO Vanco for home. The diarrhea was very 
persistent and it took until POD 21 for the ___ to normalize and 
the number and volume of stools to be tolerable.
Hemodialysis presented many challenges to fluid removal due to 
multiple factors. She was often hypotensive during the 
treatemnts and unable to have fluid removed, and on occasion 
required fluid bolus but this was at the time of multiple/large 
volume stooling.
Also, her known afib was not well controlled on the amiodarone, 
and balancing adding a beta blocker with increasing dose was the 
recommendation of the cardiology service, but this was difficult 
in the setting of hemodialysis. It was finally determined to 
hold beta blocker on the morning of hemodialysis.
The hepatology service was consulted due to patient having 
ascites develop following her surgery. They felt this was likely 
related to relative hypotension and fluid retention after 
nephrectomy, in addition to possible compression  
of portal veins. 
A liver duplex was ordered and innumerable cysts are seen 
throughout the liver including a dominant rim calcified cyst. 
The portal venous flow is normal as is the 
hepatic venous flow. There is a large amount of ascites. 
An ultrasound guided paracentesis was done on ___ with 3 
liters of fluid removed. The WBC was 70 and the labs were WNL. 
She felt much better following the paracentesis. Midodrine was 
started per renal recs and increased to 10 mg TID with good 
effects at dialysis.
She remained afebrile throughout the hospitalization once the C 
diff was identified and treated.
The clips were removed prior to discharge and steri strips 
applied. The incision looks C/D/I.
Hemodialysis was continued per schedule and she received 2 units 
of blood prior to discharge. She should continue to hold the 
beta blocker on the morning of dialysis and continue the 
midodrine as directed.
Cardiology has recommended a surface echo, to assess causes of 
the hypotension and also the intermittent Afib. This should be 
scheduled as an outpatient.

problem_prompt_block:
- Polycystic kidney, autosomal dominant
- Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
- Delirium due to conditions classified elsewhere
- Intestinal infection due to Clostridium difficile
- Candidiasis of mouth
- Congenital cystic disease of liver
- Other ascites
- End stage renal disease
- Peritoneal adhesions (postoperative) (postinfection)
- Incisional hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene
- Atrial fibrillation
- Long-term (current) use of anticoagulants
- Other specified forms of chronic ischemic heart disease
- Hypotension of hemodialysis

No comparison studies available.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of hemorrhage, mass, mass effect, or
infarction. There is no shift of midline structures. The ventricles are normal
in size. The sulci are normal in configuration.  

The middle ear cavities and included portions of the mastoid cells are clear.
Included portions of the paranasal sinuses are clear.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intracranial process.

COMMENT:  Findings were communicated by Dr. ___ to Dr. ___ at 9:30 a.m.
on ___.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH

INDICATION:  Decreasing O2 saturation, bilateral nephrectomy.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  Today's radiograph is after abdominal surgery.  Clips are seen
projecting over the abdomen, there is free subdiaphragmatic bilateral air.

Unchanged moderate cardiomegaly, minimal retrocardiac and bilateral basal
atelectasis.  No evidence of focal parenchymal opacity suggesting pneumonia. 
No evidence of pneumothorax.  No overhydration.

INDICATION:  ___ female with mental status changes.  Postop day two
from bilateral native nephrectomies.

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal short TR, short TE spin echo images were obtained through
the brain.  Axial imaging was performed with long TR, long TE, fast spin echo,
FLAIR, gradient echo, and diffusion technique.  Three-dimensional time-of-
flight MR arteriography was performed.

COMPARISON:  CT of the head available from ___.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of hemorrhage, edema, masses, mass effect, or
infarction.  The ventricles are normal in size.  The sulci are normal in
configuration.  No diffusion abnormalities are detected.

There is a hypoplastic right vertebral artery which is minimally visualized
distal to the origin of the right ___.  Just proximal to the ___
there is narrowing of the vertebral artery that extends distally to the
proximal right ___. This may be due to a focal stenosis, or a non-occlusive
thrombus at the branch point.

The left ___ arises from the left ascending pharyngeal artery. There is no
communication with the left vertebral artery, which otherwise appears normal.
This represents an anatomical variation with no clinical significance.  

The bilateral internal carotid arteries and their major branches appear normal
without evidence of stenosis, occlusion, or aneurysm formation.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No acute hemorrhage or infarction seen.  No diffusion abnormalities
detected.
2.  Stenosis of the right vertebral artery at the origin of the ___, with
some narrowing involving proximal segment of the ___. This may relfect a
focal stenosis or a nonocclusive thrombus.
3. Left ___ arising from the left ascending pharyngeal artery.

COMMENT:  Initial findings were discussed by Dr. ___ to Dr. ___ at 2:00
p.m. on ___.

Note that there are simple avascular fluid collections seen in the bilateral

IMPRESSION:

1.  No evidence of bilateral lower extremity DVT.

2.  Bilateral fluid collections in the popliteal fossae, most compatible with

ABDOMEN, TWO VIEWS:  There is air in non-distended bowel loops.  There is no

are noted.  An ovoid calcific density overlying the right hemipelvis most

1.  Numerous hepatic cysts consistent with history of polycystic kidney
disease.  Normal portal venous and hepatic venous flow.

2.  Large amount of ascites.  An appropriate spot for paracentesis was marked
in the right lower quadrant.

INDICATION:  A ___ woman with ascites and large hepatic cyst.

PROCEDURE:  After the risks, benefits and alternatives to the procedure were
discussed with the patient, written informed consent was obtained.
Preprocedure timeout was performed per ___ protocol using two patient

chosen in the right lower quadrant.  This area was prepped and draped in the
usual sterile fashion.  Local anesthesia was achieved using buffered lidocaine
solution the subcutaneous and deeper tissues.  A ___ ___ catheter then
was inserted into the peritoneal cavity.  Three liters of clear fluid were
obtained.  There was no immediate post-procedure complications.  The patient
tolerated the procedure well.

Dr. ___ radiologist, was present for the key portions of the

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You're here today for your scheduled bilateral nephrectomy due to your polycystic kidney disease. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit nervous, but I’ve been in pain for months. I can’t bend or move well. I just want relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The surgery should help with the pain and mobility. We’ll remove both kidneys and repair the hernias we know about. The procedure is complex due to adhesions, but Dr. ___ will be doing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on dialysis right after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start hemodialysis as scheduled. Your access is ready. We’ll monitor you closely, especially for blood pressure changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from surgery. The bilateral nephrectomy and hernia repair went well. The kidneys were very large—about 8 kg total. We spared your adrenal glands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I feel groggy, but no pain yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing okay overall, but we noticed you were more lethargic this morning and your temperature is up to 101.6. We’re concerned and ordering a brain MRI to rule out stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stroke? But I didn’t have weakness or slurred speech.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s reassuring. But confusion after surgery can be a sign, so we’re being cautious. We also drew blood cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the MRI and MRA of your head showed no stroke, bleeding, or blockage. Your mental status change isn’t from a brain issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s causing the confusion then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. It could be from infection, medications, or your body adjusting after surgery. Blood cultures are still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative. No infection in the blood. But we’re starting your first hemodialysis session today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. I felt dizzy during dialysis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. You did get a bit hypotensive, so we gave a fluid bolus. We’re adjusting the plan with cardiology to manage your atrial fibrillation and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed diarrhea. We sent a stool test for C. difficile, given your recent antibiotics and hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been watery and frequent. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your condition. We’re starting Flagyl while we wait for results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The test came back positive for C. diff. We’re upgrading to dual therapy—IV Flagyl and oral vancomycin—for better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need this at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Infectious disease recommends continuing oral vancomycin after discharge to prevent relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis was tough again—you dropped pressure and needed fluids. This is partly due to the diarrhea causing fluid loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology suggests holding your atenolol on dialysis mornings to avoid low BP. We’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still having ascites—fluid in your belly. Hepatology thinks it’s from low blood pressure and possible liver cyst compression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be making me feel bloated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A liver ultrasound showed normal blood flow but many cysts and a lot of fluid. We may need to drain some.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff diarrhea is still severe. We’re continuing the dual antibiotics. The vancomycin is helping, but slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so tired from going to the bathroom all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re supporting you with fluids and monitoring electrolytes. It should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A repeat abdominal X-ray shows no bowel obstruction. Your liver cyst is still there, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests today show improvement. No more C. diff toxin. But we’re keeping you on vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the infection is responding. But the diarrhea hasn’t fully stopped yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still having ascites. We’re starting midodrine to help with blood pressure and dialysis tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me keep fluid off during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. It helps your blood vessels stay constricted, so you’re less likely to drop pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a paracentesis today—drained 3 liters of fluid from your abdomen. You should feel less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel better. My breathing is easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The fluid wasn’t infected—WBC was low. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has finally improved. Stools are less frequent and more formed. That’s a big milestone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe it’s been over two weeks. I’m so glad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. You’ll continue oral vancomycin at home for two more weeks to prevent relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture showed some yeast, but it’s likely just from your mouth. No treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had mouth sores. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll keep an eye on it. Good oral hygiene is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your incision looks great—no redness or drainage. We removed the clips and put on steri-strips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels better. No pain with movement now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’ve come a long way—surgery, infection, dialysis challenges, and ascites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready for discharge. We’re sending you home with services. You’ll continue dialysis as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take amiodarone, warfarin, levothyroxine, sevelamer, simvastatin, Prilosec, aspirin, and midodrine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And continue the oral vancomycin for two more weeks. Take atenolol later in the day, not on dialysis mornings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever, chills, worsening diarrhea, belly pain, or swelling. Also if you can’t keep food or meds down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Cardiology wants a surface echo to check your heart function and help explain the low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis team will draw labs weekly until stable. They’ll adjust your meds based on results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. We’re proud of your progress. Take care, and call with any concerns.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for bilateral native nephrectomy due to symptomatic polycystic kidney disease causing pain and limited mobility. The surgery was performed successfully, but the postoperative course was complicated by delirium, C. difficile colitis, persistent diarrhea, hypotension during hemodialysis, and postoperative ascites. She was treated with IV and oral vancomycin for C. diff, underwent paracentesis for symptomatic ascites, and was started on midodrine to improve dialysis tolerance. Atenolol was adjusted to be taken later in the day to avoid dialysis-related hypotension. She gradually improved, with resolution of infection and stabilization of volume status. She was discharged home with services on a regimen including oral vancomycin, midodrine, and adjusted antihypertensive and anticoagulant therapy, with follow-up planned for echocardiography and ongoing dialysis management.
